items.title: Hard Lefschetz for the deformed operator on B_x B_s, in the three cases
items.statement:
The hard Lefschetz theorem for $L_\zeta$ on $M=B_x^RB_s^R$ holds in the following three cases.

(1) $\zeta>0$ and $xs<x$: under $\mathrm S(x)$, $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ implies $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$. The $\mathrm{hL}(x)$-only descent implication, with the same matrix and without an assumed $\mathrm S(x)$, is retained as an after-induction consequence in the character theorem, where $\mathrm S(x)$ has already been proved.

(2) $\zeta>0$ and $xs>x$: if $\mathrm S(\le x)$, $\mathrm{HR}(z,t)$ for all $z<x$ and simple $t$ with $zt>z$, $\mathrm{HRbar}(<x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ hold, then $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$ holds.

(3) $\zeta=0$ and $xs>x$: if $\mathrm S(\le x)$, $\mathrm{HR}(z,t)$ for all $z<x$ and simple $t$ with $zt>z$, $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ and $\mathrm{hL}(z)$ for all $z<xs$ hold, then $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$ holds.

In the remaining case $\zeta=0$ and $xs<x$, centered hard Lefschetz fails: in the decomposition $B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$ the operator $L_0$ is diagonal, the bottom vector of the first summand lies in degree $-\ell(x)-1$ and its $(\ell(x)+1)$-st $\rho$-power is zero, while the opposite total degree is nonzero by self-duality; the two copies have Lefschetz strings centered at $-1$ and $+1$ rather than at zero.
items.strategy: Case (1): apply the local simple-invariants descent lemma under S(x). It gives B_x=N⊗_{R^s}R and the explicit reduced matrix [[rho,0],[zeta rho(alpha_s^vee),rho]] on B_x(1)⊕B_x(-1). The local supplier proves hL by an explicit binomial power calculation on each primitive rho string tensored with the centered two-dimensional string; the middle matrices have determinant 1 and the extreme map is multiplication by the nonzero integer m+1. At zeta=0 the bottom class b∈B_xbar^{-ell(x)} has degree -ell(x)-1 in B_x(1)bar and rho^{ell(x)+1}b=0, giving failure of centered hL. Case (2): put x=s_1...s_m, gamma_i=(s_{i-1}...s_1 rho)(alpha_{s_i}^vee)>0 and gamma_{m+1}=(x^{-1}rho)(alpha_s^vee)+zeta rho(alpha_s^vee)>0. The deleted-word factorization and chosen minimal-complex embedding give <b,L_zeta b'>=<phi b,phi b'>_gamma for the first differential phi:F_xF_s^0=B_xB_s→(^1F_x)B_s⊕B_x(1). After reduction it commutes with L_zeta on the first target and rho on B_x(1); the extra right zeta rho term on the second target vanishes. Reduced cohomology makes phi injective in degrees ≤ell(x). With W=(^1F_x)(-1)B_s⊕B_x, the map lands in W(1). The unshifted (^1F_x)(-1) has the induced HR signs by the Rouquier supplier, and its lower indecomposable summands satisfy HR(y,s)_zeta; the tensoring lemma gives HR on its B_s product. HR(x) supplies the other orthogonal target component. Positive rescalings preserve signs, so the weak-Lefschetz substitute gives injectivity of every L_zeta^k, and self-duality gives equal source/target dimensions. Case (3): take the same positive gamma scalars with zeta=0 and split (^1F_x)(-1)=B_up⊕B_down orthogonally, with summands B_y satisfying respectively ys>y and ys<y. The descent supplier applies to lower y since S(y) is known. Cancel the contractible tau_{≤-2}(B_down B_s(1)) against the next differential by the perverse lower-bound supplier; the remaining first differential is d=(d_1,d_2,d_3):B_xB_s→B_x(1)⊕B_up B_s(1)⊕B_down and remains injective in degrees ≤ell(x). All components commute with left rho. For a nonzero b in degree -k, if d_3(b)≠0, the assumed hL on every lower B_y gives rho^k d_3(b)≠0 and hence rho^k b≠0. Otherwise put V=ker d_3 and W=B_x⊕B_up B_s. The map (d_1,d_2):V→W(1) is injective in negative degrees and form-compatible: the removed shifted-descent piece has identically zero Lefschetz forms by the degenerate-shift lemma, so <phi b,phi b'>=<b,rho b'> on V. HR on W follows from HR(x), HR(y,s) for the ascent summands and the tensoring lemma. The weak-Lefschetz substitute gives rho^k injective on V^{-k}. These two cases give hL on the whole source by dimension symmetry. No step assumes HR for the unseparated zero-parameter descent target, and no step invokes the unconditional singular-category descent theorem.

items.title: Simultaneous induction: Soergel's conjecture, hard Lefschetz and the Hodge-Riemann relations hold for all elements
items.statement:
Let $X\subseteq S_n$ be a finite Bruhat ideal containing the initial ideal $X_0=\{w:\ell(w)\le2\}$ and assume:

(1) $\mathrm{HR}(z,t)_\zeta$ holds for all $\zeta\ge0$, all $z<zt$ with $zt\in X$ and all simple $t$;

(2) $\mathrm{HR}(z,t)_\zeta$ holds for all $\zeta>0$, all $zt<z$ with $z\in X$ and all simple $t$.

Then for every $x\in X$ the three statements $\mathrm S(x)$, $\mathrm hL(x)$ and $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ hold. The length-ordered induction below starts with the unit, establishes (1) and (2) on $X_0$ in its first two length layers, and preserves them as each next element is adjoined. It therefore gives: for every $w\in S_n$, Soergel's conjecture $\mathrm S(w)$, hard Lefschetz $\mathrm hL(w)$ and the Hodge-Riemann relations $\mathrm{HR}(w)$ hold; and for every $x,s$ with $xs>x$ the strong forms $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_\zeta$ hold for all $\zeta\ge0$. The induction below is finite (it runs over the finitely many elements of $S_n$) and uses no choice.
items.strategy: Assemble the four implications proved in the previous items: (i) S(<xs) and S^\pm(<xs,x,s) imply S(xs) (detection + embedding theorem); (ii) S(<xs) and HR(x,s) imply S^\pm(<xs,x,s) (embedding theorem, definiteness of subspaces of definite forms); (iii) S(<=x) and HR(<=x, lower) imply hL(x,s)_zeta for all zeta >= 0 (the three-case hard Lefschetz theorem); (iv) HR(x) and hL(x,s)_zeta for all zeta imply HR(x,s)_zeta for all zeta (large-deformation theorem + signature constancy). The passage from HR(x,s) to HR(xs) is the restriction to a direct summand and Lemma 2.2; the passage from HR(x,s)_zeta for all zeta to S(xs) uses the embedding theorem and the detection theorem. Base of the induction: X_0 = {w : \ell(w) <= 2}: for ell(w) <= 1 the computation is the rank-one example, for ell(w) = 2 (both sides in type A_2 inside S_n, or the degenerate case where w is a product of two distant reflections) the character and the Hodge-Riemann signs are checked directly from the rank-two decompositions and the rank-one forms. The induction is finite (S_n is finite) and uses no choice. Every passage from the tensor product to its top B_xs summand uses zeta=0, following deformation back to zero, and invokes the undeformed restriction lemma; never restrict the positive middle-position operator without an invariant-summand proof. For descent pairs keep the parameter interval (0,∞): choose a sufficiently large positive starting parameter and apply signature constancy on a compact interval joining it to the requested positive parameter. For ascent pairs use [0,∞) after the separate zero-parameter proof. Thus the descent failure at zero has no effect on the simultaneous induction. The base cases are calculated within the A proof (the elementary rank-one and two-factor forms); the B examples are illustrations and not prerequisites.

items.title: Soergel's character conjecture for type A
items.statement: For every $w\in S_n$ the character of the indecomposable type-$A$ Soergel bimodule equals the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element: $\operatorname{ch}(B_w^R)=\underline H_w$. Equivalently, the class $[B_w^R]$ in the split Grothendieck group corresponds to $\underline H_w$ under the Hecke algebra isomorphism, and the extension of scalars of the rational $B_w$ categorifies the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis. Moreover the hard Lefschetz property $\mathrm hL(w)$ and the Hodge-Riemann relations $\mathrm{HR}(w)$ hold for every $w$, with the standard signs, and the same identities hold for the rational category by the base-change comparison. Finally, for every right descent $xs<x$ the matrix of $L_\zeta$ on $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}\rho\cdot(-)&0\\ \zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)&\rho\cdot(-)\end{pmatrix}$; for $\zeta>0$, $\mathrm hL(x)$ implies $\mathrm hL(x,s)_\zeta$ without any additional character hypothesis, since $\mathrm S$ is now established for all elements, while at $\zeta=0$ centered hard Lefschetz fails.
items.strategy: Apply the simultaneous induction theorem with X = S_n: it gives S(w) for all w, i.e. ch(B_w^R) = H_w by the definition of S(w) in the dictionary of hypotheses. The identification of the character with the class in the split Grothendieck group is the multiplicativity and the Hecke isomorphism of the published type-A Soergel page; the comparison with the rational category is the base-change lemma. No positivity is assumed from the published Kazhdan-Lusztig basis item; only its existence and triangularity are used to name H_w. Only after the simultaneous induction gives S(w) for every w, apply the local simple-invariants descent lemma and the positive-descent case of the deformed hard-Lefschetz theorem to obtain the unrestricted descent consequence. Thus the induction itself uses the conditional descent lemma solely on already-established lower subjects, and the stronger consequence creates no logical cycle.

items.title: Positivity of Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials, mu-coefficients and structure constants
items.strategy: (1) By the character theorem ch(B_w^R) = H_w and by definition of the character the coefficient of H_y in ch(B_w^R) is the polynomial \Sigma_d (B_w : Delta_y(d))v^d with all multiplicities in Z_{>=0}; comparing with the expansion of H_w in the standard basis gives h_{y,w} = \Sigma_d(B_w:Delta_y(d))v^d, hence non-negative, and the classical normalization gives the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials. (2) Since the class map sends [B_z^R] to H_z (character theorem), the equality [B_x^R][B_y^R] = [B_x^R \otimes_R B_y^R] in the split Grothendieck group and the decomposition of the tensor product into indecomposables give H_xH_y = \Sigma_z m_zH_z with m_z in Z_{>=0}[v^{\pm1}]; the multiplicativity of the character over R is part of the base-change comparison. (3) is the same computation read in the standard basis, using that the filtrations of the tensor product have non-negative multiplicities. All uses are finite and choice-free.

items.title: The rank-two Bott-Samelson bimodule B_sB_t: character, decomposition and the braid relation
items.statement:
Take $n=3$ and the two simple reflections $s=s_1$, $t=s_2$. The rank-two Bott-Samelson bimodule $B_sB_t$ has character
$$\operatorname{ch}(B_sB_t)=\operatorname{ch}(B_s)\operatorname{ch}(B_t)=(H_s+v)(H_t+v)=H_{st}+vH_s+vH_t+v^2$$
in the standard basis, so its $\Delta$-multiplicities are $1$ at $H_{st}$, $1$ at $H_s$ and at $H_t$ with shift $v$, and $1$ at the identity with shift $v^2$; in particular all multiplicities are non-negative and $\dim(\overline{B_sB_t})=1+1+1+1=4$. In $S_3$ the product $st$ has length $2$ and $B_{st}$ has the same character $\underline H_{st}=H_{st}+vH_s+vH_t+v^2$, so $B_sB_t=B_{st}$ is already indecomposable; equivalently the only summand is the top one $B_{st}$ and all multiplicities $m_y$ for $y<st$ vanish. Similarly $B_sB_tB_s=B_{sts}\oplus B_s$ with characters $\underline H_{sts}+\underline H_s$, whereas $B_tB_sB_t=B_{sts}\oplus B_t$; the two Bott-Samelson products are not isomorphic; the example also verifies the rank-two values of the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials $P_{e,st}=P_{s,st}=P_{t,st}=1$ used on the companion page.
items.strategy: Use the multiplicativity of the character (published type-A standard character) with the rank-one values ch(B_s) = H_s+v and ch(B_t) = H_t+v (the rank-one example). Expand the product in the standard basis using H_sH_t = H_{st} (reduced product) to get H_{st}+vH_s+vH_t+v^2. Compute the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element H_{st} on this page by bar-invariance and triangularity (as in the rank-one computation but one step higher: bar(H_{st}) = H_{st}+(v-v^{-1})(H_s+H_t)+v^2-2+v^{-2}) to get H_{st} = H_{st}+vH_s+vH_t+v^2, which coincides with the character; hence B_{st} is the unique indecomposable with this character and B_sB_t is indecomposable. The braid relation for B_sB_tB_s follows from the published rank-two decomposition theorem, and the multiplicities m_y for y < st are read off from the equality of the two characters: all vanish. Record that the reduction to rank two is essential here (the design requires the examples to stop at rank two and forbids their use in the general induction).

items.title: The coinvariant algebra of S_3 as the Soergel bimodule of the longest element
items.statement:
Take $n=3$ and let $w_0=s_1s_2s_1$ be the longest element of $S_3$. Then $B_{w_0}=S\otimes_{S^{S_3}}S(3)$ and its reduced module is $C(3)$, where $C=S/(S^{S_3}_+)$ is the unshifted coinvariant algebra: $C$ has the Poincare polynomial $1+2t^2+2t^4+t^6$, so $\dim C=6$, and in the centered grading
$$\dim(\overline{B_{w_0}})^{-3}=\dim(\overline{B_{w_0}})^{3}=1,\qquad \dim(\overline{B_{w_0}})^{-1}=\dim(\overline{B_{w_0}})^{1}=2 .$$
The standard-basis expansion of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element is
$$\underline H_{w_0}=H_{w_0}+v(H_{s_1s_2}+H_{s_2s_1})+v^2(H_{s_1}+H_{s_2})+v^3,$$
obtained by solving the bar-invariance and triangularity conditions with coefficients in $v^d\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; its coefficients are non-negative, its value at $v=1$ sums to $6=\dim C$, and it agrees with the rank-one and rank-two Kazhdan-Lusztig data $P_{e,w_0}=P_{s_i,w_0}=P_{w,w_0}=1$ for $\ell(w)=2$. Hence $\operatorname{ch}(B_{w_0})=\underline H_{w_0}$: Soergel's conjecture holds for the longest element of $S_3$, and the $\Delta$-multiplicities of the coinvariant bimodule are the six coefficients just displayed, one for each element of $S_3$.
items.strategy: Identify B_{w_0} with S \otimes_{S^{S_3}} S(3): for a finite Weyl group the longest indecomposable Soergel bimodule is the tensor product over the invariants (use the published rank-two longest-bimodule supplier, not a single graph bimodule), and its reduction is the coinvariant algebra by the Chevalley-Shephard-Todd theorem; compute the Poincare polynomial by the classical invariant-theoretic count (1+t^2)(1+t^2+t^4). Compute the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element H_{w_0} by the elementary algorithm: solve for a bar-invariant element of the form H_{w_0} + \Sigma_{y<w_0}a_yH_y with a_y in vZ[v], using bar(H_{w_0}) computed from H_{w_0} = H_{s_1}H_{s_2}H_{s_1} and bar(H_s) = H_s + v - v^{-1}; the solution has a_{s_1s_2} = a_{s_2s_1} = v, a_{s_1} = a_{s_2} = v^2 and a_e = v^3. Then compare with the Delta-filtration of the coinvariant algebra: the six layer multiplicities are the coefficients of H_{w_0}, and the sums match the Hilbert function in the centered grading. Record explicitly that the two sides agree term by term and that no positivity of Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials is assumed (the coefficients are computed directly).

items.title: Hard Lefschetz fails for a non-dominant degree-two element: the rank-one case
items.statement:
In the rank-one case $n=2$ the element $\rho':=x_1+x_2$ is a degree-two element
of $S$ with $\rho'(\alpha_s^\vee)=0$, so it is not strictly dominant. Its action
on the reduced rank-one Soergel module is zero: $\rho'=e_1=x_1+x_2$ is
$s$-invariant and of positive degree, and $x_1+x_2=1\cdot e_1$ acts on the right
basis element $\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}}$ as the right action by an element of
$S_+$, hence $\rho'\cdot\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}}=0$; a fortiori it cannot map
$(\overline{B_s})^{-1}=\mathbb R\,\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}}$ isomorphically to
$(\overline{B_s})^{1}$. Therefore for $\rho'$ the hard Lefschetz property fails
(the map on the $-1$ degree is the zero map), even though $\rho'$ is a symmetric
degree-two endomorphism of the reduced module; the same failure occurs for every
degree-two element with $\rho'(\alpha_s^\vee)=0$. Consequently the hard Lefschetz and Hodge-Riemann conclusions do not hold
for arbitrary degree-two elements when strict dominance is omitted. This does
not assert that every Lefschetz element is strictly dominant.
items.strategy: For n=2, rho'=x_1+x_2 is s-invariant and has rho'(alpha_s^vee)=0 in the coordinate root normalization. In B_s=S⊗_{S^s}S(1), its invariance gives rho'⊗1=1⊗rho' exactly by the balanced tensor relation. Left rho' thus equals right rho' on the whole bimodule and acts as zero after right reduction. Both degree -1 and +1 reduced spaces have dimension one, so the degree-one Lefschetz map is zero and fails hL. More generally any degree-two rho' with rho'(alpha_s^vee)=0 has equal coordinate coefficients and is a scalar multiple of this invariant; the same argument applies. The bottom Lefschetz form is identically zero as well.

items.title: The rank-one Soergel bimodule: trace form, reduced module and hard Lefschetz
items.statement:
Take $n=2$, so $S_n=\{e,s\}$ and $B_s=B_s^R=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$ with $S=\mathbb R[x_1,x_2]$, $\deg x_i=2$ and $\alpha_s=x_1-x_2$. In the right $S$-basis $\{c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\}$ of degrees $-1$ and $+1$ the multiplication relations are
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}},\qquad c_{\mathrm{id}}c_s=c_s,\qquad c_sc_s=c_s\alpha_s .$$
The trace is $\operatorname{Tr}(c_{\mathrm{id}}a+c_sb)=b$ for $a,b\in S$ and the intersection form has the Gram matrix
$$\begin{pmatrix}\langle c_{\mathrm{id}},c_{\mathrm{id}}\rangle&\langle c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\rangle\\ \langle c_s,c_{\mathrm{id}}\rangle&\langle c_s,c_s\rangle\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&\alpha_s\end{pmatrix},$$
whose determinant is $-1$, so the form is non-degenerate, and the induced form on the reduced module is non-degenerate too. The reduced module has the real basis $(\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}},\overline{c_s})$ with degrees $-1$ and $+1$, so $\dim(\overline{B_s})^{-1}=\dim(\overline{B_s})^{1}=1$; for $\rho=\alpha_s/2=(x_1-x_2)/2$, which is strictly dominant with $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)=1$, one computes $\rho\cdot\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}}=\overline{c_s}$ and $\rho\cdot\overline{c_s}=0$. Hence $\rho:(\overline{B_s})^{-1}\to(\overline{B_s})^{1}$ is an isomorphism, hard Lefschetz holds, the primitive subspace in degree $-1$ is all of $(\overline{B_s})^{-1}$, and the Lefschetz form $(a,b)=\langle a,\rho b\rangle$ is positive on it: $\langle\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}},\overline{c_s}\rangle=1>0$, matching the Hodge-Riemann sign $(-1)^{(\ell(s)-1)/2}=+1$. Finally $\operatorname{ch}(B_s)=H_s+v=\underline H_s$, the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element of the simple reflection, which is Soergel's conjecture at $s$, and the rational model over $\mathbb Q$ gives the same numbers.
items.strategy: Compute the right-linear trace with right coefficients c_id a+c_s b; Gram matrix [[0,1],[1,alpha]]; rho=alpha/2, partial_s(rho)=1; reduction gives a length-two Lefschetz string and positive bottom value. Direct graph kernel and quotient give ch(B_s)=H_s+v without the global character theorem.

items.title: Hard Lefschetz and the Hodge-Riemann signs for the coinvariant algebra of S_3
items.statement: For $n=3$ identify the centered reduced longest-element module with $C(3)$, where $C=\mathbb R[x_1,x_2,x_3]/(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ has dimensions $1,2,2,1$ in degrees $0,2,4,6$, so that the centered degrees are $-3,-1,1,3$. For every strictly dominant $\rho$ hard Lefschetz is the pair of isomorphisms $\rho^3:C(3)^{-3}\to C(3)^3$ and $\rho:C(3)^{-1}\to C(3)^1$. The primitive spaces used in the Hodge-Riemann relations are $P^{-3}=C(3)^{-3}$ of dimension one and $P^{-1}=\ker(\rho^2:C(3)^{-1}\to C(3)^3)$ of dimension one; their Lefschetz forms are respectively positive and negative definite, and the primitive decomposition consists of one length-four $\rho$-string and one length-two $\rho$-string. For an explicit strictly dominant choice let $x=x_1$, $y=x_2$, $x_3=-x-y$, $\rho=x_1-x_3=2x+y$ and normalize $\operatorname{Tr}(x^2y)=1$. Then $C=\mathbb R[x,y]/(x^2+xy+y^2,x^3)$, with basis $1;x,y;x^2,xy;x^2y$; the $\rho$-map from degree $2$ to degree $4$ has the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, $\rho^3(1)=6x^2y$, $P^{-1}=\mathbb Ry$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(y\rho y)=-2$. These computations verify hard Lefschetz and the primitive signs directly in rank two.
items.strategy: Eliminate e_1 by x_3=-x-y. The remaining relations are x^2+xy+y^2=0 and x^2y+xy^2=0, equivalently x^2+xy+y^2=0 and x^3=0. Reduction gives the six displayed basis elements; their dimensions agree with the invariant-ring count, proving independence. The trace normalization is the positive standard top trace (the divided difference ∂_{w_0}(x^2y)=1). Compute rho x=2x^2+xy and rho y=-x^2+xy, so the middle Lefschetz map has determinant 3. The relations imply xy^2=-x^2y and y^3=0, hence rho^3=6x^2y. Also rho^2x=3x^2y and rho^2y=0, so the primitive kernel in centered degree -1 is exactly R y; its Lefschetz value is Tr(y rho y)=-2. The bottom primitive Lefschetz value is Tr(rho^3)=6. All other vectors lie in the two primitive strings and are not new HR primitive spaces. To cover arbitrary strictly dominant rho=a x+b y after removing its invariant component, dominance means a>b>0. The middle determinant is a^2-ab+b^2>0, rho^3=3ab(a-b)x^2y>0, and for p=a(a-2b)x-b(2a-b)y one has rho^2p=0 and Tr(p rho p)=-3ab(a-b)(a^2-ab+b^2)<0. These formulas give the full dominant-chamber verification without relying on the example as an induction supplier.
